761.event_title: Gustavus Adolphus's reformed Swedish army wins at Breitenfeld
761.event: At Breitenfeld, the Swedish-Saxon army under King Gustav II Adolf of Sweden met the imperial and Catholic League army under Count Tilly. When the Saxon contingent fled, the Swedes reordered their lines to form a new left flank, outgunned the enemy in the artillery exchange, and destroyed Tilly's army. It was the first major Protestant victory of the Thirty Years' War and established Sweden as a great power.
761.explanation: Britannica credits the victory to Sweden's flexible, well-drilled linear tactics, the product of Gustavus's reforms of infantry, cavalry and artillery working together.
761.tie_back: The kural ranks first among a king's treasures an army complete in all its parts that wins without fearing harm, and at Breitenfeld a well-integrated Swedish army held firm even when its allies ran.
761._accuracy_note: A strong example of a complete, disciplined army as a kingdom's chief asset, though the kural's claim is about ranking treasures rather than a single battle.

762.event_title: The Ten Thousand march home after losing their generals
762.place: From Cunaxa near Babylon (Iraq) to Trapezus (Trabzon, Turkey)
762.event: A force of Greek mercenaries known as the Ten Thousand fought for Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa in 401 BCE, but Cyrus was killed and the expedition failed. Their senior generals were then seized through treachery by the Persian satrap Tissaphernes during a parley. The soldiers elected new leaders, among them the Athenian Xenophon, and marched north through hostile mountains and snow-filled passes until they reached the Black Sea at Trapezus.
762.explanation: Stranded deep in enemy territory, leaderless and dwindling, the army kept its cohesion and fought its way out, a story Xenophon recorded in the Anabasis.
762.tie_back: The kural says the courage to hold firm in defeat and loss of numbers is found mainly in a seasoned army, and the veteran Ten Thousand did exactly that after disaster had stripped them of their cause and their commanders.
762._accuracy_note: A vivid case of steadiness in defeat; the Ten Thousand were seasoned veterans rather than the hereditary core troops Parimelazhagar has in mind.

763.event_title: Robert the Bruce's smaller army defeats Edward II at Bannockburn
763.place: Bannockburn, near Stirling, Scotland, United Kingdom
763.event: Edward II of England led a large army, estimated at some 13,000 infantry and about 3,000 cavalry, to relieve the besieged Stirling Castle. Robert the Bruce met it with a smaller force of perhaps 7,000 infantry, mostly pikemen, and a few hundred light horse, using woodland and dug ditches to channel the attack. Repeated English cavalry charges failed to break the Scottish spear formations, and the English army was routed, with Edward barely escaping.
763.explanation: A disciplined, determined smaller force overthrew a far larger and more splendid host, in what Britannica calls a decisive battle in Scottish history.
763.tie_back: The kural asks what it matters if a host of rats roars like the sea when a single breath of the cobra scatters them, and at Bannockburn the larger army's numbers counted for little against the resolve of the smaller one.
763._accuracy_note: A good fit for numbers yielding to courage, though the English were not timid and terrain and tactics also decided the battle.

764.event_title: The Swiss Guard's stand during the Sack of Rome
764.place: St Peter's Basilica, Rome (now Vatican City)
764.event: When the troops of Emperor Charles V stormed Rome, 189 men of the Pontifical Swiss Guard defended Pope Clement VII. Of these, 147 were killed, many on the steps of St Peter's, while the pope escaped to Castel Sant'Angelo. New recruits to the Swiss Guard have been sworn in each year on 6 May in commemoration of that day.
764.explanation: The Guard held to its duty to the end rather than abandon or betray the pope, and the corps has kept that memory as its living tradition for five centuries.
764.tie_back: The kural names as a true army one that cannot be won over by the enemy and that carries courage handed down through generations, and the Swiss Guard's loyalty and its yearly oath on the anniversary embody both.
764._accuracy_note: Loyalty and inherited courage fit well, but the Guard was nearly destroyed, which sits awkwardly with the kural's first mark of an army never broken.

765.event_title: The Knights of St John hold Malta against the Ottoman siege
765.event: In May 1565 a large Ottoman force landed on Malta to take the island from the Knights Hospitaller under Grand Master Jean de Valette. The much smaller garrison of knights, soldiers and Maltese defenders held out for nearly four months, losing Fort St Elmo but keeping the main fortifications. When a relief force from Sicily landed in September the Ottomans withdrew, and Malta still marks 8 September as a public holiday.
765.explanation: Britannica notes that the defence halted the Ottoman advance into the western Mediterranean and shattered their reputation for invincibility.
765.tie_back: The kural says that is truly an army which can stand together and face the foe even if Death himself comes raging, and Malta's defenders held as one through months when death was daily expected.
765._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of collective resolve under near-certain death.

766.event_title: Twenty-one soldiers of the 36th Sikhs defend Saragarhi
766.place: Saragarhi, Samana Range, North-West Frontier (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
766.event: Saragarhi was a small signalling post linking Fort Lockhart and Fort Gulistan, held by twenty-one men of the 36th Sikhs under Havildar Ishar Singh. When thousands of Orakzai and Afridi tribesmen attacked, the garrison refused to surrender and fought until all were killed. All twenty-one were posthumously awarded the Indian Order of Merit, then the highest gallantry award open to Indian soldiers, and the Sikh Regiment marks 12 September as Saragarhi Day.
766.explanation: The defenders were trusted with a vital post and kept that trust with valour and honour that their regiment still commemorates every year.
766.tie_back: The kural names valour, honour, following the noble path of predecessors and being trusted as an army's four safeguards, and the Saragarhi garrison displayed all four in a single day.
766._accuracy_note: A close match to the four named qualities; the battle ended in the garrison's death, so it illustrates character more than outcome.

767.event_title: The 93rd Highlanders' Thin Red Line at Balaklava
767.event: During the Battle of Balaklava a body of Russian cavalry advanced toward the British base, and the 93rd Highlanders, about 500 men under Sir Colin Campbell, stood in its path. Instead of forming the usual four-deep square, Campbell drew them up in a line two deep, and their disciplined volleys turned the Russian horsemen back. The Times correspondent William Howard Russell's description of them gave rise to the phrase the thin red line.
767.explanation: A single steady regiment took the full weight of the enemy's leading charge and stopped it.
767.tie_back: The kural praises an army that knows how to withstand an oncoming attack and bears the brunt of the enemy's vanguard, which is precisely what the 93rd did at Balaklava.
767._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a line meeting and turning back the enemy's leading assault.

768.event_title: Zheng He's treasure fleets sail to the Indian Ocean
768.place: From Nanjing, China, to South-East Asia, India, the Persian Gulf and East Africa
768.event: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court sent seven great expeditions under the eunuch admiral Zheng He, with fleets far larger than any then sailing, to South-East Asia, India's Malabar Coast, Hormuz and the coast of East Africa. The fleets carried gifts and were armed, but their chief purpose was diplomatic. On his return in 1415 Zheng He brought envoys of many states of South and South-East Asia to pay homage to the emperor.
768.explanation: The sheer scale and splendour of the fleets carried Ming prestige across the Indian Ocean and drew many rulers into tributary relations, largely without war.
768.tie_back: The kural says that even without using its strength to attack or defend, a force can win renown by the splendour of its array, and Zheng He's fleets won China honour chiefly by being seen.
768._accuracy_note: A good illustration of prestige won through display; the fleets were naval and diplomatic rather than an army, and did fight on a few occasions.

769.event_title: The Pennsylvania Line mutinies over pay and enlistments
769.place: Morristown and Princeton, New Jersey, United States
769.event: On the night of 1 January 1781 soldiers of the Pennsylvania Line in the Continental Army, long unpaid and poorly supplied and insisting their enlistments had expired, rose in mutiny at their winter camp near Morristown, and an officer was killed in the disorder. Some 1,500 men marched toward Princeton to press their demands on Congress, while rejecting British offers of pardon and back pay to change sides. The mutiny was settled by negotiation, with many men discharged and others furloughed.
769.explanation: Even loyal troops who refused to desert to the enemy could no longer function as an army once pay, supplies and goodwill toward their government had run out.
769.tie_back: The kural says an army wins if it is free from dwindling numbers, lasting discontent and want, and the Pennsylvania Line shows what happens when discontent and poverty take hold.
769._accuracy_note: A clear counter-example: the kural's conditions for victory, unmet, nearly dissolved a whole state line.

770.event_title: Darius III flees and his vast army collapses at Gaugamela
770.event: At Gaugamela the Persian king Darius III faced Alexander the Great with an army far larger than the Macedonian force, on a plain he had levelled for his chariots and cavalry. When Alexander drove toward Darius's position, Darius fled the field, as he had at Issus two years earlier. The Persian army broke and was routed, and Alexander went on to take Babylon, Susa and Persepolis.
770.explanation: A huge army of brave soldiers fell apart once its commander abandoned the field, deciding the fate of the Persian Empire.
770.tie_back: The kural says that however many steadfast soldiers an army has, it cannot stand without worthy leaders, and Gaugamela shows a mighty host dissolving when its leader failed.
770._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of an army that could not stand once its leadership failed; ancient numbers are uncertain and one cuneiform source frames the flight differently.
